$comment: Controlled vocabulary of skeletal and soft-tissue attachment sites. Every `attachments` reference in data/muscles-*.json resolves to an `id` here. Three things this buys that a free-string list did not: (1) `partOf` gives the bone-first browse a drill-down (pectoral girdle -> scapula -> acromion); (2) `presence` records where an element is absent, so the interface can show that a muscle's attachment had to move rather than silently dropping the row; (3) `correlate: true` marks sites that leave a recognisable osteological trace, which is the entry point for fossil reconstruction. Presence statements are sourced; where a source is not yet attached the claim is standard comparative anatomy and flagged `sourced: false`.

presence.note:
Scored present in Crocodylia and Aves on three descriptive sources, resolving a contradiction this record carried while it was scored mammal-only. Meers (2003) names it repeatedly as a crocodylian scapular landmark with its own lateral surface, not in passing: the deltoideus clavicularis takes a fleshy origin from it along the cranial margin of the scapula, and the supracoracoideus brevis from the lower part of its lateral surface. Schreiweis (1982) gives three penguin muscles an origin on the acromial process of the scapula — deltoideus major, the short dorsal head of deltoideus minor, and the dorsal head of triceps scapularis. Widrig et al. (2023) describe the tinamou acromion projecting cranially from the scapula. Their 'acromial process of the furcula' is a different structure sharing the word, and is still not evidence either way — but it is not the only acromion they describe, which is why this record previously dismissed them.

**Scored on topological correspondence, not demonstrated homology.** In archosaurs the acromion is the cranial process of the scapula at the clavicle/furcula contact; in therians it is the distal end of the scapular spine, which is itself a therian novelty. The two occupy the same position and carry the same deltoid-series origins, which is the basis used here, and it is the same standard this project applies to muscle homology groups. None of these sources demonstrates that the therian acromion and the archosaur one are the same structure, and a source that separates them should be followed over this row. Lepidosauria and Testudines are left unscored: no source here names an acromion in either, and that is unrecorded rather than absent. **Testudines added on Walker (1973)**, who names it as a discrete ramus of the triradiate turtle scapula and puts two muscles on it: the deltoideus arises from its anterior surface, the anterior head of the supracoracoideus from its ventral surface and posterior border. That is the third clade this record has gained since it was scored mammal-only, and the second time a descriptive source has contradicted the original scoring.

elements.label: Angular / ectotympanic
elements.transformation: A postdentary dermal bone that becomes the ring supporting the mammalian tympanic membrane.

elements.label: Articular / malleus
elements.transformation: The ossified posterior end of Meckel's cartilage. It meets the quadrate at the jaw joint in non-mammals and becomes the malleus in mammals — the partner of the quadrate/incus, moving into the ear together with it.

presence.note: The fin articulation on the scapulocoracoid. Diogo et al. (2016) use it as the landmark separating dorsal (adductor) from ventral (abductor) muscle origins — the fish equivalent of the glenoid.

The fused proximal tarsal of squamates and turtles. Added because Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) put attachments on it that cannot be assigned to the astragalus or the calcaneum separately — the adductor hallucis dorsalis arises from a convex lip at the proximolateral margin of its tarsal facet in Iguana, and the extensor hallucis proprius from its dorsal aspect in Chelydra. `fusedFrom` rather than a second name for the astragalus, on the same reasoning as the avian carpometacarpus.
Its hollow carries the origin of the extensor digitorum brevis superficialis in Caiman.
Its reduction is one of four character complexes Werneburg & Maier (2019) tie to the akinetic turtle skull.

An anteroposterior ridge on the lateroventral coracoid, most prominent anteriorly. Named by Walker (1972) and treated as homologous across early crocodylomorphs by Crush (1980); Bodenham et al. report it in Galahadosuchus and compare it with Terrestrisuchus and Dromicosuchus. Scored only for the stem column because no source here identifies it in crown Crocodylia.
Rostral origin of the adductor internus in anurans, medial to the eye.

The dorsal shell. Load-bearing for myology, not just for defence: in *Pseudemys* the latissimus dorsi arises from it along a line running from the scapular articulation out over the first pleural plate, and the testocoracoideus from its margin beside the limb notch. A turtle has trunk muscles originating from a bone no other tetrapod has.

One bone in the proximal carpal row of monotremes, identified by Holmgren (1952) as fused radiale + intermedium + centrale. It takes the insertion of the brachioradialis, on a dorsal projection between its joints with distal carpals II and III, and the prepollex articulates with it. A `fusedFrom` case rather than three separate rows, on the same reasoning as the avian carpometacarpus.

elements.label: Carpometacarpus

presence.note: Fused distal carpals and metacarpals in birds. Its processus extensorius carries the insertion of the extensor metacarpi radialis and its caudodorsal proximal surface that of the extensor metacarpi ulnaris, so it is the element most avian wing extensor rows land on.

elements.transformation: Distal carpals fused with metacarpals II-IV; the alular metacarpal (digit I) remains distinguishable within the compound, which is why sources name an 'alular metacarpal' and a 'major metacarpal' on one bone.

presence.note: Origin of the caudofemoralis and of the tail-to-girdle muscles. In Taricha the caudofemoralis takes the fourth and fifth caudal transverse processes — a countable segmental address, which makes this one of the few attachment sites that can be scored by position along the column rather than by bone alone.
Replaced by the urostyle in anurans and shortened to the pygostyle in birds — both associated with caudofemoralis reduction.
The manual counterpart of centrale-pes. Carried here chiefly as a component of the monotreme preaxial carpal complex, which fuses it with the radiale and the intermedium.
Central tarsal of the primitive tetrapod ankle, retained in salamanders.

Cieri (2018) reports three to four in most varanids examined. Monotremes keep free cervical ribs on all six post-atlantal cervicals, and Gambaryan et al. (2015) hang the whole serratus ventralis cervicis on them — one slip per rib, C2 to C7. The rib of the axis, which they call the epistropheal rib, also carries two of the three portions of the levator scapulae.
A distinct cervical series requires the girdle to be freed from the skull, which happens with the loss of the cleithrum along the tetrapod stem.
Reduced or absent in many cursorial mammals; fused into the furcula in birds.
Dermal element linking the pectoral girdle to the skull in fishes. Its loss along the tetrapod stem is what frees the girdle from the head and permits a neck.
Where present, carries much of the abductor superficialis origin in teleosts.
Proximal tibial crest receiving the knee extensor tendon; prominent in archosaurs.

Two different absences. In the fishes and stem tetrapodomorphs there is no separate coracoid because the girdle is an undivided scapulocoracoid; `derivedFrom` carries that homology. In therians it is a genuine loss — an independent ossification surviving only as the coracoid process of the scapula, which forces the origin of the supracoracoideus onto the lateral scapula and removes the coracoid head of the subcoracoscapularis. That second case is the clearest example in the dataset of an attachment moving because its bone disappeared.

A circular depression near the posterior margin of the lateroventral coracoid, present in Galahadosuchus, Dromicosuchus (NCSM 13733) and Terrestrisuchus. Crush (1980) read it as the coracobrachialis anterior attachment.

All that remains of the coracoid in therians, fused to the scapula. Muscles that arose from the coracoid bone in other tetrapods — biceps brachii and coracobrachialis — arise from this process instead.
The ceratobranchial of a fish and the cornu branchiale of a salamander or turtle are one element under two names. The ventral gill-arch muscles of eels run from it to the hypobranchials.
Tendinous sheet receiving much of the adductor complex in turtles.
Incorporated into the mammalian middle ear or lost as the dentary takes over the jaw joint.
Crest running posteriorly from the proximal anuran femur, carrying the insertion of the iliofemoralis on its dorsal surface.

The lateral ridge of the otic capsule, and the caudal limit of the jaw-adductor origin in frogs. Johnston (2011) runs the adductor mandibulae longus back onto it, which is what makes the origin field of that muscle a resolvable site rather than 'the back of the skull'.

The single most useful osteological correlate in the pectoral appendage. Its presence and shape is the primary evidence for reconstructing the pectoralis, supracoracoideus and deltoid complex in fossil taxa.
The sole bone of the therian lower jaw; elsewhere one of several, with the postdentary series carrying part of the adductor insertion.
The rib-bearing facet on the transverse process. Origin of the levator costae in varanids, which is one of the two muscles connecting each rib independently to the vertebral column.
Blotto et al. (2020) refer the origin of most anuran intrinsic hand muscles to the fused distal carpal 3-4-5.
Distal tarsal row. Origin of the intrinsic pedal muscles — the serial counterpart of the distal carpal row in the manus.

Read as the brachioradialis ('supinator longus') insertion in Ossinodus. There is no break in the muscle scarring between this ridge and the proximoventral ridge, so Bishop's two insertions may not be separate muscles' worth of scarring at all.
An anuran carpal element receiving the extensor carpi radialis tendon.

Dorsal elements of the branchial arches, numbered 1-4 in teleosts. Added because the dorsal gill-arch muscles run between them — a levator externus onto its own epibranchial, a rectus dorsalis from one onto the PRECEDING one — and `branchial-arches` as a single group cannot express that. Extended to Chondrichthyes for the cucullaris, which Ziermann et al. report inserting on the posterior epibranchials as well as on the girdle.

Cartilaginous medial part of the anuran pectoral girdle, carrying the origin of the pars episternalis of the deltoid. Present in lizards too, where Molnar et al. record the subcoracoideus arising from it, but no row here uses that yet.

The ossified ascending process of the palatoquadrate. Werneburg & Maier (2019) show it forms the secondary lateral braincase wall in cryptodire turtles, while pleurodires build that wall from the descending process of the parietal instead, having no extended ascending process to ossify.
Anterior cartilaginous extension of the turtle pubis; carries part of the puboischiofemoralis internus origin.

Cartilage rods lying lateral to the branchial arches proper, outside the gill pouches. In Squalus the anterior ones take the cucullaris and the intermediate constrictores branchiales; in Petromyzon the arcus extrabranchialis takes the adductores and compressores. Held as one element because Ziermann et al. use one name for both, but the lamprey branchial basket is external and continuous where the gnathostome arches are internal and segmental, and whether the two are the same structure is unsettled. Do not read a shared element id here as a homology claim.
The varanid trochanter receiving the caudofemoralis; homologous with the fourth trochanter of archosaurs.
The proximo-distal series of the metapterygial axis. Its first and second elements correspond to the tetrapod stylopod and zeugopod; the pronator and supinator series attach segmentally along it.
No tetrapod counterpart. The tetrapod autopod is a novelty rather than a transformed radial series — see Diogo et al. (2016) on the distal tendon primordium.
Bony vertebral portion plus a costal cartilage that does not reach the sternum.

Origin correlate for the m. interosseus dorsalis digiti II — the one member of that series birds retain, as m. abductor digiti II (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021). Re-parented from `metatarsals` to `tarsometatarsus`: it is scored in Aves only, and the avian metatarsals are the tarsometatarsus, so a row naming this landmark on the loose metatarsals could not resolve.

The best single fossil-muscle landmark in the vertebrate skeleton. It carries the caudofemoralis, so its size reads directly as femoral-retractor power, and its independent reduction in birds and loss in mammals marks two separate departures from tail-driven locomotion. Godoy et al. (2016) identify it in the baurusuchid Pissarrachampsa as a rough convexity continuing distally as a faint ridge — much less prominent than the crocodylian condition.
Chen et al. (2025) score this region across crown birds in an osteological character matrix; their scoring conventions are the reference for how these elements are delimited here.
Insertion field for the superficial branchial constrictors, which compress the pharynx during the expulsion phase of the respiratory cycle.

Small bone of the posterior urodele lower jaw, associated with Meckel's cartilage, and the insertion of every visceral jaw opener Bauer describes. Added because scoring those muscles on `mandible` generally would lose the distinction he draws between the depressor mandibulae reaching it DIRECTLY and the ceratomandibularis reaching it only through a ligament.
The connective-tissue sheet dividing epaxial from hypaxial musculature. It is the boundary that defines the two, and it is marked by the split of the spinal nerve into dorsal and ventral rami.

Flagged as a correlate on histological rather than inspectional evidence: Pereyra et al. (2019) section the humerus of three turtles and find Sharpey's fibres at the insertions of the latissimus dorsi with teres major, the deltoideus, the subscapularis and the pectoralis, and at the origins of the triceps and brachialis, across the proximal metaphysis, diaphysis and distal metaphysis. Read their Table 2 for what the flag does NOT license — the triceps origin marks the diaphysis in two of the three species and not the third, so a smooth humerus is not an absent muscle. See METHODS.md.

The turtle humerus carries two proximal processes rather than the tubercles of other amniotes. The lateral takes the pectoralis and the supracoracoideus; it shifts distally in sea turtles, which Walker reads as increasing the adductor moment arm.
Takes the subscapularis insertion in *Pseudemys*.

elements.label: Hyomandibula / stapes
elements.transformation: One element throughout. The hyomandibula braces the jaw joint against the braincase in fishes; with the tetrapod jaw suspension it is freed and becomes the sound-conducting columella, and the stapes of mammals. The muscle acting on it followed it the whole way — the depressor hyomandibulae of a shark is the stapedius of a mammal, still on the facial nerve.

presence.note: Carries most of the ceratomandibularis insertion in Necturus, which is why that muscle reaches the gonial indirectly. A muscle end that leaves no osteological trace, like the midventral raphe of the shark and the humeral feather tract of the loon.

Ventral elements of the branchial arches, between the ceratobranchials and the basibranchial series. Springer & Johnson make one of them a character: hypobranchial 3 is cartilaginous or absent in eels and largely ossified in all other elopomorphs and most other teleosts, which they identify as an anguilliform synapomorphy not previously noted.
Landmark on the fibular shaft; the fibularis longus arises distal to it.

Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of the iliofemoralis/gluteal field and is central to Bishop & Pierce's (2024) argument that erect posture was acquired late.

Present from the stem tetrapods onward; scars on its ventral surface, distinct from the dermal ornament, are tentatively read as part of the origin of superficial ventral muscles such as the pectoralis. Retained in monotremes, which is a large part of why the monotreme pectoralis has a more extensive origin than the therian one.
Proximal carpal between radiale and ulnare, retained in salamanders and reduced or fused in most amniotes. Serially corresponds to the tarsal intermedium but is a separate element.
Proximal tarsal between tibiale and fibulare. Serial counterpart of the carpal intermedium; separate element for the same reason radiale and tibiale are separate.

The groove between the proximal humeral processes. In *Pseudemys* the coracobrachialis brevis inserts into it and the biceps tendon forms at its level, so it is a site rather than only a passage for tendons.

The common aponeurotic sheet over the anuran knee. Several thigh muscles that in other tetrapods reach bone insert here instead, so a large part of the anuran thigh leaves no osteological trace at its distal end.

Common origin of the extensor (dorsal-mass, radial-innervated) forearm musculature throughout Tetrapoda. **Deliberately carries both names in the label rather than a `taxonNames` entry.** The ecte-/ent- and lateral/medial pairs split by author tradition, not by taxon, so a per-taxon name would assert a pattern that is not there. Ercoli et al. (2014) use ectepicondyle for a mustelid; Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) use lateral epicondyle across the sauropsids; Molnar et al. (2018) use ecte-/ent- throughout the tetrapod stem. Counted over the extracted sources the palaeontological and comparative literature prefers one pair and the mammalian-clinical the other, and both appear inside single clades. The synonym is the right home for the alternative. The chelonian literature calls it the **radial epicondyle** — Walker (1973) uses that pair throughout, naming the bone the muscles run toward rather than the side of the body they sit on. A third naming tradition on the same two landmarks.

Proximal dorsal humerus. One or more oblique ridges in Tiktaalik, Panderichthys and Acanthostega; a distinct, often spike-like process in later stem tetrapods such as Baphetes and Pederpes. Its appearance at the last common ancestor of Elpistostegalia is what Molnar et al. read as the separation of the latissimus dorsi from the deltoideus. Absent in Eusthenopteron and Gogonasus, and disputed in the rhizodontids: Jeffery (2001) reads the Strepsodus and Rhizodus processes as part of the ventral ridge or as breakage. Recorded under this name only for the stem taxa surveyed here — the homologue in Iguana is an unnamed prominence.

The crista tuberculi minoris, running distally from the tubercle onto the shaft. Separated from the tubercle itself because the two carry different muscles and the distinction is the observation: in all three monotreme genera the subscapularis takes the proximal apex of the tubercle while the subcoracoideus and teres major descend along the crest below it (Gambaryan et al. 2015).

The cartilage bar carrying the hagfish dental plates, and the anchor the protractors and retractors of the feeding apparatus pull on. Ziermann et al. distinguish anterior, middle and posterior lingual cartilages and the pharyngolingual arch; only the anterior/posterior distinction is scoreable here, by side. Not the gnathostome tongue skeleton, and not scored for lampreys — the lamprey piston cartilage is a separate question this source does not settle.
The anteriormost ray, served by its own arrector muscles in teleosts — the first differentiation out of the abductor-arrector anlage.
Occupied by section Aω of the teleost adductor mandibulae.

elements.label: Meckel's cartilage
elements.transformation: The endoskeletal core of the lower jaw, present in every jawed vertebrate. In chondrichthyans it IS the lower jaw; in bony fishes and tetrapods a series of dermal bones ensheaths it, and it persists inside them.

presence.note: Common origin of the flexor (ventral-mass) forearm musculature. Diogo & Molnar (2014) follow Sigurdsen & Bolt (2009) in reidentifying the salamander 'ulnar condyle' of Francis (1934) as the entepicondyle. **Deliberately carries both names in the label rather than a `taxonNames` entry.** The ecte-/ent- and lateral/medial pairs split by author tradition, not by taxon, so a per-taxon name would assert a pattern that is not there. Ercoli et al. (2014) use ectepicondyle for a mustelid; Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) use lateral epicondyle across the sauropsids; Molnar et al. (2018) use ecte-/ent- throughout the tetrapod stem. Counted over the extracted sources the palaeontological and comparative literature prefers one pair and the mammalian-clinical the other, and both appear inside single clades. The synonym is the right home for the alternative. The chelonian literature calls it the **ulnar epicondyle** — Walker (1973) uses that pair throughout, naming the bone the muscles run toward rather than the side of the body they sit on. A third naming tradition on the same two landmarks.

Fine striae, longitudinal or parallel to the metatarsal long axis, marking the origins of the deep pedal series. Pereyra et al. (2024) identify these as pedal muscle correlates for the first time; because they vary little between crocodylian species they are usable on fossil archosaurs.

Median connective sheet of the floor of the mouth. Both halves of the intermandibularis and the interhyoideus insert on it rather than on cartilage, so the whole ventral sheet of the mandibular and hyoid arches leaves nothing skeletal behind.
Segmental connective-tissue partitions between myomeres. Tetrapod axial muscles lose strict segmental septation as they reorganise into longitudinal tracts.
Insertion of the triceps throughout Tetrapoda; a reliable fossil indicator of elbow extensor leverage.
Cartilaginous plate in the fenestra ovalis. Target of the opercularis, a pectoral-girdle muscle that inserts on the ear — the amphibian substrate-vibration pathway.
Origin surface of the teleost adductor mandibulae.

elements.label: Palatoquadrate / quadrate
elements.transformation: The upper jaw cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch. Its posterior end ossifies as the quadrate and carries the jaw joint in non-mammals; in mammals it leaves the jaw entirely and becomes the incus, which is why the mammalian jaw joint is squamosal-dentary instead of quadrate-articular.

elements.label: Palmar sesamoid

presence.note: The os sesamoideum flexorium commune, a sesamoid in the common tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus at the point where it divides into digital branches. Gambaryan et al. coin the Latin term and cite Ponssa et al. (2010) that the bone itself is common across tetrapods; it is scored `variable` rather than `no` for that reason, and listed present only where a source has actually reported it. It is a real attachment site and not an incidental ossicle: in Tachyglossus the common tendon inserts on its proximal apex and the digital branches leave its distal end, and in Ornithorhynchus there are two of them, a medial one giving the tendons of digits I-III and a lateral one those of digits IV and V.

synonyms: os sesamoideum flexorium commune (Gambaryan et al. 2015)

presence.note: The tongue skeleton of birds, carried on the front of the hyoid apparatus. Most of the intrinsic tongue musculature attaches to it, so it is where the avian hypobranchial rows land.
Principal origin surface for the adductor mandibulae in taxa with an open or emarginated temporal region.
Independently acquired in birds and mammals; a sesamoid in the knee extensor tendon.
Insertion correlate for the pedal extensor series; recognisable in fossils.
Most dorsal elements of the branchial arches, carrying the upper pharyngeal toothplates and the insertions of the levatores interni and the transversus dorsalis.
The ventral shell, and the origin of the pectoralis, which in *Pseudemys* sweeps an arc from the midventral line back to the bridge.

Posterior flange or ridge confluent with the olecranon, present in every stem tetrapod here whose ulna is preserved and absent in tetrapodomorph fish. Molnar et al. read the pair of features as the separation of the triceps from the extensor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris at the last common ancestor of Tetrapoda. The crest itself is a boundary between the dorsal and ventral forearm musculature rather than an attachment, so no muscle is scored on it.
Pedal counterpart of the prepollex, with its own abductor and flexor musculature in anurans.

A preaxial element medial to digit I. In anurans it carries its own musculature — adductor pollicis, a contrahens, flexores breves profundi slips — so it behaves as a digit even though it is not one. Relevant to the position-versus-identity argument: anurans lost digit 1 yet the preaxial muscles found something to attach to. **Monotremes have one too, and it carries more muscle than the anuran one.** Gambaryan et al. (2015) put the whole insertion of the flexor carpi radialis on it in all three genera, and the origins of the interossei of digits I to III; in Zaglossus its pull is relayed on to the distal carpals and metacarpals I-III by ligaments. So the preaxial element carrying its own musculature is not an anuran peculiarity — it is present in a mammal, in an animal that did NOT lose digit I.

Carries the origin of the procoracohumeralis — the amphibian name for what amniotes call the deltoideus clavicularis. The muscle is renamed for the bone, not for any change in the muscle. **Retained in monotremes, and it is not a vestige**: Gambaryan et al. (2015) put the origins of the supracoracoideus, the subcoracoideus and both heads of the biceps brachii on it, and the sternocoracoideus and costocoracoideus insert on it. Five muscles on a bone therians do not have, which is most of why the monotreme girdle cannot be read off a therian one.
Read as the extensor carpi radialis insertion in Ossinodus. See the dorsomesial ridge for why the two insertions may not be separate.
Ramus of the fish pelvic plate. Diogo et al. (2016) record several pelvic fin muscles arising from its dorsal, medial and caudolateral faces.

elements.label: Pygostyle
elements.transformation: The distal caudal vertebrae fused into a single plate.

presence.note: Cartilage at the corner of the mouth carrying the levator anguli oris. In colubroid snakes it is elaborated into the venom gland, which is why parts of the levator anguli oris there insert on the gland rather than the plate.

The sacrum is a tetrapod novelty: fishes have no vertebrae fused to a pelvic girdle, because the pelvic fin girdle floats free of the axial skeleton. Fusing them is what lets a hindlimb transmit thrust to the body.

Absent as a separate element wherever the undivided scapulocoracoid is the girdle — the fishes and the stem tetrapodomorphs — and absent altogether in the agnathans, which have no paired appendages. `derivedFrom` carries the homology, so a muscle scored on the scapulocoracoid is still reachable from here.

The angulus caudalis, the posterodorsal corner of the scapular blade. Four muscles converge on it in monotremes — the teres major and one slip of the latissimus spinalis arise there, and the serratus ventralis thoracis and the caudal portion of the rhomboideus insert there. **Scored absent outside the mammals as a fact about names, not about bone.** Every tetrapod scapular blade has corners; only the mammalian literature names them, so an attachment row here cannot be written for a lizard even where the same corner carries the same muscle.

The craniodorsal corner of the scapular blade, opposite the caudal angle. Carries the origin of the spinodeltoideus and the insertion of the cranial portion of the rhomboideus in all three monotreme genera. Same nomenclatural caveat as the caudal angle.

The dorsal process of the chondrichthyan scapulocoracoid, rising free above the fin articulation. It is where the cucullaris lands, so it carries the only attachment in this dataset that crosses the head-trunk boundary onto the girdle — the anatomical fact the whole protractor pectoralis record exists to hold.

The dorsal ramus of the triradiate turtle scapula, distinct from the acromion on the same bone. Walker (1973) hangs the deltoideus, teres major and subscapularis on it, so it carries three muscles and is worth separating from `scapula` generally.
A therian novelty. Incipient in monotremes, which is why the monotreme shoulder is the readable intermediate: it divides the ancestral supracoracoideus field into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
Endoskeletal pectoral girdle of fishes, bearing the articular process for the fin. It is the element that becomes the separate scapula and coracoid of tetrapods.

Depression proximal and anterior to the latissimus dorsi attachment on the dorsal humerus, taken as the procoracohumeralis insertion — Coates's 'scapulohumeralis-like muscle' in Acanthostega. Described elsewhere as a shallow concavity, or as a rugose ridge behind one.
The reduced first (mandibular) gill slit. Its pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, and the region keeps trigeminal innervation throughout.
Carries the spiracularis insertion with the distal hyomandibula, forming the anterior wall of the spiracular valve.

Carries both the pectoralis and the supracoracoideus. The whole flight apparatus is powered from below the centre of mass because the supracoracoideus tendon is redirected dorsally through the foramen triosseum. Chen et al. (2025) score this region across crown birds in an osteological character matrix; their scoring conventions are the reference for how these elements are delimited here.

The ligament the urodele ulnocarpalis inserts on. It matters here because it is the diagnostic structure in Gambaryan et al.'s (2015) argument that the same muscle survives in mammals: in Ornithorhynchus its postaxial segment persists as the ligamentum flexorium commune transversum, running from the ventral side of the ulnare to the medial palmar sesamoid, and its deeper sheet as the ligamentum palmaris profundum, crossing from pisiform and ulnare to the prepollex. Kajava (1911) reports the transverse ligament in Tachyglossus as well, apparently as individual variation, and Straus (1942) in some lipotyphlan insectivores. Scored present only in the two clades a source describes it in; a muscle end, not a bone, so its absence elsewhere is largely unrecorded.

The ledge of the chondrichthyan neurocranium below the orbit, and the origin of the adductor mandibulae posterior in Callorhinchus. Dearden et al. resolve it by synchrotron tomography, which is how a jaw-muscle origin gets a named site in an animal with no bone to leave a scar on.

Convex process on the anterior edge of the humerus, two-thirds of the way along in Acanthostega and often continuing as a ridge toward the ectepicondyle. It is confluent with the deltoid process as a single deltoid-supinator ridge in Eusthenopteron, Gogonasus, Barameda and Rhizodus, which Molnar et al. treat as leaving the deltoideus and brachioradialis attachments indistinguishable — for muscle reconstruction the long argument over whether the two processes are separate in those taxa changes nothing. Read as the brachioradialis ('supinator longus') origin from Eryops onward.
Cartilaginous dorsal extension of the scapula. Its loss in mammals shifts several axio-appendicular insertions onto the scapular border itself.
Major adductor insertion surface in non-mammalian tetrapods.

The longitudinal bars that tie the lamprey branchial basket together, running fore-and-aft across the segmental cartilages rather than within one arch. Scored by side: `dorsal` is the taenia longitudinalis epitrematica above the gill openings, `ventral` covers both the hypotrematica below them and the mid-ventral taenia longitudinalis ventralis. No gnathostome counterpart — a lattice of this kind is what the branchial basket is, and it is the clearest skeletal reason not to read the lamprey basket as a set of branchial arches.

elements.label: Tarsometatarsus

presence.note: Fused distal tarsals and metatarsals II-IV in birds. Its proximal dorsal tuberosities are the insertion correlate for the m. tibialis cranialis.

elements.transformation: Distal tarsals fused with metatarsals II-IV. Metatarsal I remains free, so the metatarsal series is not wholly absorbed.

presence.note: Werneburg & Preuschoft (2024) treat the temporal bars as struts resisting the compressive and tensile stresses of biting; the pattern of openings between them follows from where those stresses run, rather than being an arbitrary taxonomic character.
Configuration of the temporal openings constrains adductor mandibulae volume and orientation; the primary osteological handle on jaw muscle reconstruction in fossils.
Elongated with the fibulare into the anuran tarsal segment that lengthens the jumping limb.

elements.label: Tibiofibula

presence.note: Fused tibia and fibula of anurans. Recorded as a compound with `fusedFrom` rather than as `partOf` either component, so a comparison against a taxon with separate bones reads as a fusion of the skeleton and not as a muscle moving.

elements.transformation: Tibia and fibula fused into a single element in anurans, one of the skeletal changes tied to the saltatory hindlimb.

elements.label: Tibiotarsus

presence.note: Fused tibia and proximal tarsals in birds.

elements.transformation: Tibia fused with the proximal tarsals (astragalus and calcaneum).

presence.note: Takes the iliofemoralis insertion in *Pseudemys*. Named on Walker's usage for turtles; not equated here with the mammalian greater trochanter, which is a separate question this dataset has not settled.
Takes part of the puboischiofemoralis internus insertion in *Pseudemys*.
Reach the sternum by a sternal portion of calcified cartilage; three in most varanids.

Dorsal prominence of the anuran iliac shaft at the junction with the acetabular portion. It carries the shared origin of the iliofibularis and iliofemoralis on its posterolateral surface and the origin of the glutaeus maximus on its dorsolateral surface — three muscles on one process, which is what makes it worth scoring separately from the ilium.
Ventral tubercle of the avian proximal humerus; receives the coracobrachialis caudalis.
Insertion of the biceps profundus in *Pseudemys*. Distinct from `biceps-tubercle`, which is on the coracoid — the two share a name and nothing else.

The terminal, claw-bearing phalanges of the hand. Reached first by the monotreme digital extensors and flexors, every one of which ends on them rather than on the phalanges generally — three muscles in three genera with three different digital formulae, which is only expressible against a distinct element.

Split from a single `ungual-phalanges` element, which was parented to the pes alone while carrying the id a manual row would reach for — the same trap that put pedal phalanges on three forelimb records before Walthall & Ashley-Ross was mined. Paired with ungual-phalanges-manus on the intermedium-manus / intermedium-pes pattern.
Fused post-sacral rod replacing the anuran tail. Its rigidity is part of the saltatory apparatus.

Anteroposterior ridge on the ventral cleithrum of Sauripterus, Gogonasus and Eusthenopteron, read as the anterior extent of the pectoralis origin. Molnar et al. homologise it with the longitudinal ridge that carries the abductor superficialis origin on the cleithrum and clavicle of Neoceratodus, on the grounds that those two muscles are themselves homologous. The cleithral attachment of the pectoralis was lost before the cleithrum was.

The undivided ventral ridge of the tetrapodomorph humerus, confluent with the entepicondyle in Gogonasus, Eusthenopteron and Tiktaalik and separate in Panderichthys. Part of it carries the pectoralis insertion. The distinct pectoralis process that separates out of it is a tetrapod character, so a row on this ridge is deliberately coarser than one on the deltopectoral crest.

elements.label: Ventral median ridge of the radius

presence.note: One of the four longitudinal ridges of the stem-tetrapod radius in Bishop's terminology, usually carrying obvious muscle scars, read as the humeroantebrachialis insertion. Molnar et al.'s character mapping puts its first appearance at the last common ancestor of crown tetrapods, where it marks the separation of the humeroantebrachialis from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis — yet their own description lists it among the ridges of the Acanthostega and Pederpes radius. The rows scored on it carry that tension.

Prominent in Ossinodus and carrying no muscle scarring itself; what Bishop reads as the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis insertion is the scarred face between it and the ventral median ridge. Possibly the 'distal ventral keel' of Eryops, and so the radial flexor ridge of Pawley & Warren.
Y-shaped cartilage projecting forward from the anterior margin of the pubis. Anchors the anterior continuation of the rectus abdominis and receives the m. ypsiloideus.
